subject: Six citizens sue Trump over White House press ban
posts: Six everyday citizens take on the White House in a bold First Amendment battle over press bans and public access. Evidence: Federal lawsuit filed in NY, independent reporting rights, executive restrictions. #Aletheia #USPol 🌐

The plaintiffs argue that executive press bans unlawfully restrict the public's constitutional right to independent information and government oversight. Stated Judgement: (+1.0, +1.0) — Greater Good Potential

Viewpoint-based press bans restrict democratic accountability and shield power from scrutiny, prompting citizens to force judicial intervention. Resulting Judgement: (-0.8, -0.7) — Exclusive Constraint

Verdict: FAIL — The Path of Deception. Executive overreach curtails public access while claiming transparency, sparking necessary judicial pushback.

Integrity: Severe Deception (Hypocrisy: 12.5, z: 4)
Citizens and news outlets are locked in constitutional litigation over White House press access, testing the limits of executive authority.
Federal courts continue to check sweeping administrative removal and press restriction powers, reaffirming the separation of powers.

The Poison:
Using selective press exclusions to punish critical coverage erodes public trust and distorts democratic accountability.
The Plane Error occurs when executive power confuses political retaliation with legitimate administrative authority, substituting viewpoint control for law.

Social Physics Analysis:
The administration runs a smart selfish maneuver, using manufactured press restrictions to punish critics while projecting grievance. Citizens counter with transparent legal action to restore democratic access.

The Trajectory: The Path of Deception.
Modal Dynamics: will be -> is not via Red Top (The Imperial Trap). Promising open governance while enacting viewpoint bans inverts democratic principle into restriction.

The Unavoidable Truth: Executive press bans impair the public's fundamental right to independent government reporting.
The Unavoidable Lie: Viewpoint-based exclusions are routine administrative measures.

Alethekanon:
Executive power cannot lawfully extinguish the public's right to independent oversight through arbitrary press bans.

Awwthekanon:
It takes immense courage for everyday citizens, educators, and historians to stand up in federal court and defend our shared right to the truth.

Brothekanon:
When the White House starts banning reporters for bad reviews, citizens stepping up with lawsuits is the ultimate receipts check.

"He who justifies the wicked, and he who condemns the just, both of them alike are an abomination to the Lord." Proverbs 17:15 FAIL
Twisting executive retaliation into lawful administration mocks justice and perverts constitutional balance.

Actual Article Body:
Six citizens who consume the news reported by the White House press corps to do their jobs are suing President Donald Trump over his press ban on CNN, Politico, and MS Now.

The individual plaintiffs join the three news outlets in filing a First Amendment lawsuit against the administration. But unlike the outlets’ case, the newly filed suit argues the press ban violates the public’s right to independent reporting and seeks to protect journalists covering the White House from retaliation more broadly.

Obama judge rules Trump DOJ illegally fired James Comey's daughter, rejects sweeping Article II claim

The Trump Justice Department fired Maurene Comey without cause, but a federal judge ruled it violated the Civil Service Reform Act and ordered backpay.

Actual Article Body:

Market data provided by Factset. Powered and implemented by FactSet Digital Solutions. Legal Statement. Mutual Fund and ETF data provided by LSEG.

Fox News legal analyst Gregg Jarrett evaluates the federal indictment of former FBI Director James Comey for an alleged threatening social media post on ‘Hannity.’

An Obama-appointed New York federal judge ruled Monday that the Trump Justice Department unlawfully fired former FBI Director James Comey's daughter Maurene, rejecting the administration's sweeping claim of executive authority and warning that its argument threatened the nation's constitutional balance of power.

The Justice Department acknowledged in court filings that Comey's firing was not for-cause and was not based on her performance, but argued that the attorney general had the authority to remove her under Article II of the Constitution.

"Defendants’ argument that [Constitution] Article II bars Congress from regulating the removal of AUSAs (assistant U.S. attorneys) flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent," Judge Jesse Furman wrote, adding that accepting the administration's argument would "unsettle the very equilibrium established by this nation's constitutional system."

TRUMP’S FIRING POWER FACES TWIN SUPREME COURT TESTS, BUT ONE AGENCY MAY GET SPECIAL TREATMENT

Former federal prosecutor Maurene Comey and her father, former FBI Director James Comey, are seen in this split image. Comey, a longtime U.S. prosecutor for the Justice Department, sued the Trump administration Monday, Sept. 15, over her abrupt firing earlier this year.  (Getty Images)

A DOJ spokesperson told Fox News Digital the department disagreed with the decision and will appeal it in "due course." Furman ordered Comey retroactively reinstated and awarded back pay through Dec. 20, 2025, when she accepted another job.

While federal law gives the attorney general authority to fire assistant U.S. attorneys, Furman ruled that Congress placed limits on that power through the Civil Service Reform Act (CSRA), which generally requires cause for termination and procedural protections for government workers.

OBAMA JUDGE HALTS TRUMP FIRING BID AS DECADES-OLD LEGAL AUTHORITY TEES UP POSSIBLE MAJOR REVERSAL

Patrice Failor (L), wife of former FBI director James Comey, is embraced by her daughter Maurene Comey as they arrive at the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia's Bryan Courthouse on October 8, 2025, in Alexandria, Virginia.  (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

The judge found that Comey's firing violated those requirements, noting that the government conceded her removal was not based on misconduct or poor performance and that she received neither advance notice nor an opportunity to respond.

Comey had served about a decade in the prominent Southern District of New York, where she worked on some of the office’s biggest cases, including the prosecution of Ghislaine Maxwell – associate and rumored partner of Jeffrey Epstein — as well as the sex trafficking trial of rapper Sean "P. Diddy" Combs.

Furman also recently rebuked the Trump administration during its efforts to deport pro-Palestinian Columbia University student activist Mahmoud Khalil, leading the federal government to argue for a change of venue to New Jersey.

The judge, nominated in 2011, previously served as a federal prosecutor in the same Manhattan U.S. attorney's office where both Comeys worked during their careers. Furman's brother, Jason, served in the Obama administration as chairman of the Council of Economic Advisers.

James Comey served as the top prosecutor at SDNY early in the George W. Bush administration, where he investigated President Bill Clinton’s controversial pardon of financier Marc Rich as well as interior designer Martha Stewart.

The younger Comey was the second in her family to be fired under Trump, after the president terminated her father as FBI director in 2017 during the Russia collusion investigation.

The elder Comey later came under fire for posting a photo of seashells on a beach arranged to form the sentiment "86 47" – with critics saying "86" was a reference to killing something, such as in restaurant lingo, and "47" referred to Trump, the 47th president.

Maurene Comey’s attorneys said in a statement to The Associated Press that their victory was "hard-earned" for both their client and all civil servants.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Prosecutor Maurene Comey, arrived at federal court for the Sean "Diddy" Combs trial on Wednesday, May 21, 2025, in Manhattan.  (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital)

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"As the court correctly held, to accept the government’s argument about unlimited executive power ‘would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this nation’s constitutional system.’ This decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: the President is not above the law," they said.

The post Nia-Malika Henderson: Trump’s Preference for White People Now ‘Out In the Open’ appeared first on Breitbart.

Actual Article Body:
Monday on CNN’s “Inside Politics,” political analyst Nia-Malika Henderson said President Donald Trump is openly revealed himself to prefer white people to black people and brown people.

Henderson said, “Yeah, yeah. He would prefer white people to black people. Listen, this was a debate and a discussion in his first term, right? When it was revealed that he said these derogatory, racist remarks about African countries, they denied it. They sort of played it down. But now it’s all out in the open. Donald Trump has revealed himself to be, you know, somebody who prefers white people to black people, to brown people. And it will be up to the audience and his voters and Republicans to decide what they do with that, right?”

She added, “I mean, I think he thinks this works, right? And in some ways, it has worked. There wasn’t any sort of, you know, illusion about what Donald Trump thought of brown people versus white people.”

Political commentator Jonah Goldberg said, “Part of the problem is just, you know, Trump loves to play this. He plays it for guests in the Oval Office. That Harry clip from from CNN saying that Trump has 98 or 99% support from self-identified MAGA.  The problem with that is self-identified MAGA is only a slice of actual Republican voters, but he thinks that’s the only thing that matters.”
